A.text:
This is Gantry, an autonomous
producer for a live sports stream.

It watches a sports data feed and the
chat, ranks and curates what matters,
and then suggests polls, or on autopilot,

simply runs them. Everything you will
see is a recorded run of the real app,
on the offline model: no keys, no network.

Here is a goal, and twenty-five
seconds of match time later,

B.text: The loop is simple to say.

A feed and a chat go into a window:
one stretch of the broadcast,

The showrunner runs it
through two subgraphs.

The action desk generates actions,
and decides whether each one goes out,
waits for a human, or is held back.

Whatever happens is written
to the LangGraph Store,

C.text:
It runs in real time, driven
by events rather than a timer.

A goal arms a window
twenty-five seconds later,
so the chat's reaction is in it.

A penalty is urgent, and
fires within seconds.

Here we push a penalty
into the feed ourselves,

and the poll is out
before the kick is taken.

If the graphs ever fall behind, triggers
ride along with the next window.

A live system sheds load;
it does not build a queue.

D.text:
Here is one window,
replayed from the real run.

Triage is a cheap gate,
because most ticks are noise.

Then the curator runs as a subgraph,
and after it the action desk,
with the poll studio inside that.

Three levels of subgraph,
and one thread per window,

so a suggestion waiting for a
human never blocks the next goal.

E.text:
Flow one is ranking and
curation, in two stages.

The first is cheap,
deterministic, and explainable:

every moment is scored with its reasons,
and the chat is cut into shards of forty
and scored in parallel with Send.

This window had 52
comments, so two shards,

then a merge. The second
stage is an editor,
a model that sees only the shortlist.

It can reorder the best of the chat, but
never rescue what the first stage hid.

F.text: The first feature is the poll.

A moment becomes a candidate:
a topic, the facts,

Three writers, an analyst, a hype
voice, and a fan from the terraces,

A judge scores each draft:
is it clear, neutral,

And if a model ever writes nonsense, the
engine's own wording goes out instead.

G.text:
Then policy decides, for
every action: publish,

One poll at a time, a gap between
polls, never the same question twice,
never a topic the human rejected.
A big moment can close a small poll early.

And every refusal is written
to the ledger with its reason.

That record is what
lets it run on its own.

H.text:
In manual mode, every
action waits for a human.

Each suggestion is its own interrupt,
so they can be answered in any order,

by id. Here I edit the
question and publish it,

and it goes live at once,
without waiting for the others.

I reject the highlight, and
the ledger records who decided.

Each answer resumes the
graph from its checkpoint,

and nothing above the
interrupt runs twice.

I.text:
When a poll closes, the memory
keeper files how it did,
and updates what this audience votes on.

After a few matches, a disputed
decision pulls 37% of viewers,

The next candidates are
ranked on that evidence,

and when it is clear enough,
a lesson is written down.

Play the same match again, and the
second time it asks fewer questions,
and gets more votes per poll.

J.text:
It ships with an eval gate:
offline, about five seconds.

Against hidden ground truth, moment
ranking scores at least 0.96,

and 94% or more of the comments
it highlights are good.

Spam and abuse is held every time,
and none of 2,551 good comments

Over three whole matches on
autopilot: no overlapping polls,

And with memory, the second pass
gets 26.6% of viewers voting,

K.text: That is Gantry: seven LangGraph graphs,

a live feed in, polls and pins out,
and a ledger so it can be left alone.
Run make dev, and open it on localhost,

port twenty-thirty, or open
the graphs in LangGraph Studio.
These recordings used the offline model.

A real model is one setting away, and
that path is written, but not yet run.
